+# ADR 0001: Pricing Cache TTL
+
+## Status
+Accepted
+
+## Context
+
+The pricing service currently caches responses with a time-to-live (TTL) of 900 seconds (15 minutes). This relatively short cache window was initially chosen to balance freshness guarantees with query load reduction, assuming pricing updates would be frequent and require rapid propagation to clients.
+
+In practice, pricing changes are infrequent and coordinated through our deployment process. During that time, we already have mechanisms to invalidate or refresh caches at the application level. Meanwhile, the 15-minute window creates unnecessary backend pressure during peak traffic periods, as cache hits drop significantly after the 12-15 minute mark in many user sessions. Analysis of cache hit rates and backend load patterns shows that extending the TTL would provide material relief without meaningful freshness trade-offs.
+
+## Decision
+
+We are raising the pricing cache TTL from 900 seconds to 3600 seconds (1 hour). This decision applies to the pricing API response cache and should be implemented consistently across all pricing service instances and replicas.
+
+The longer window aligns with our operational practices: pricing updates are deployed infrequently, announced in advance, and handled through coordinated cache invalidation when they do occur. A one-hour window captures the vast majority of user sessions and provides a substantially improved cache hit ratio without requiring clients to interact with stale pricing data in normal operations.
+
+## Consequences
+
+Cache hit rates are expected to improve by 25-35% during peak traffic windows, reducing queries to the pricing backend by an estimated 40-50 qps at p95. This will lower latency variance for pricing requests and reduce database load, improving overall system reliability during traffic spikes.
+
+However, pricing changes will take up to 60 minutes to propagate to all clients in the absence of active invalidation. This requires discipline in our deployment process: pricing updates must be coordinated, validated before deployment, and announced with sufficient lead time. If emergency pricing changes are needed, we must manually trigger cache invalidation across all service instances. Operations and product teams should establish a clear policy for pricing change notifications and invalidation procedures.
